$comment: GENERATED by scripts/point-codec-fixtures.ts. Do not edit by hand — regenerate. Hand-copied vectors are what let the epoch-t crash through.
nonFiniteComment: nonFiniteVectors spell every channel as a string so NaN and ±Infinity survive JSON: parse with Double(_:) / toDouble() / Number(). A non-finite channel is written as the wire's zero for that channel of that point, and nothing else changes — not the point's other channels, and not any later sample.

vectors.name: empty
vectors.why: A stroke with no points still has a header: version, flags, count.

vectors.name: single
vectors.why: One point, no optional channels: the smallest real payload.

vectors.name: edges
vectors.why: Both ends of every channel's range, exactly on the boundary.

vectors.name: xyOnly
vectors.why: Position-only stream: the flags byte must omit all four optional channels.

vectors.name: withTime
vectors.why: Time channel present, the other three absent.

vectors.name: full
vectors.why: All six channels, ascending and descending tilt.

vectors.name: backtrack
vectors.why: A stroke doubling back: large negative deltas, which is what zigzag is for.

vectors.name: epochTimestamp
vectors.why: An epoch-millisecond t (~1.8e12) overflows the Int32 time channel. Swift traps on the conversion, JS does not. This is the exact input that killed the iOS app on the first point of the first stroke, and no hand-written vector used a large t.

vectors.name: epochTimestampStroke
vectors.why: Epoch t across a whole stroke: every sample clamps to the same ceiling, so every delta after the first is zero. Pins that the clamp is per-sample and not a one-off guard on the head.

vectors.name: timeAtInt32Ceiling
vectors.why: t exactly at the clamp, and one millisecond past it. Off-by-one at a clamp boundary is where a clamp is usually wrong.

vectors.name: timeGoingBackwards
vectors.why: A non-monotonic clock: the time channel takes large negative deltas, which only zigzag makes cheap. A wall clock corrected mid-stroke produces exactly this.

vectors.name: timeZeroThroughout
vectors.why: Every t identical: the whole channel is zero deltas, and the flags byte must still declare it present.

vectors.name: twoPoints
vectors.why: The minimum a freehand commit is allowed to carry.

vectors.name: draftCap
vectors.why: Exactly maxDraftPoints (180). The count crosses into a two-byte varint at 128, which no hand-written vector reached.

vectors.name: commitCap
vectors.why: Exactly maxCommitPoints (1200), all six channels. The longest stroke the protocol accepts, and a three-byte count varint. Also the case where an accumulating delta bug shows up: a drift of one unit per sample is invisible at 8 points and 1200 units at the end of this.

vectors.name: sparsePressure
vectors.why: Some points carry pressure and others do not. The codec normalises to 'all present' with the missing ones defaulting to 0 — a per-point presence bitmap costs more than it saves — and that normalisation is exactly the kind of rule two implementations drift on.

vectors.name: tiltXOnly
vectors.why: One tilt axis without the other: flag 4 set, flag 8 clear.

vectors.name: tiltYOnly
vectors.why: The mirror of the above: flag 8 set, flag 4 clear. Channel order is X, Y, T, PRESSURE, TILT_X, TILT_Y, so a reader that assumes the two tilts arrive together decodes this into garbage.

vectors.name: pressureOnly
vectors.why: Pressure with no time: flag 2 alone.

vectors.name: outOfRange
vectors.why: Every channel past both ends of its range. Clamping keeps the stream decodable instead of producing values the server rejects.

vectors.name: negativeZero
vectors.why: -0 in a channel that clamps at 0. `-0 < 0` is false so the clamp passes it through, and Math.round(-0) is -0 while Swift's (-0.0).rounded() is -0.0: both must quantise to the same 0.

vectors.name: roundingHalves
vectors.why: Values landing exactly on .5 after scaling. JavaScript's Math.round breaks ties toward +Infinity and Swift's .rounded() breaks them away from zero — identical only because every quantised value here is non-negative. That invariant is load-bearing and this is what pins it.

vectors.name: maximalDeltas
vectors.why: Alternating corner to corner: every position delta is the full 65535, the widest varint the position channel can produce.

vectors.name: subQuantumMotion
vectors.why: Motion finer than the 1/65535 grid: every delta quantises to zero, so the stroke must encode as a stationary point rather than as noise.

vectors.name: tiltQuantisation
vectors.why: Tilt across its full 180-degree span in single-step increments, which is where the 255-step scale rounds most often.

nonFiniteVectors.name: nanMidStroke
nonFiniteVectors.why: The shipped defect, stated as bytes: one NaN x at index 1 of 4. It must cost its own sample and nothing else. The old encoder wrote a zero delta and left `previous` NaN, so index 2's delta was destroyed too, and the decoder's running total stayed short for the rest of the channel: this stroke decoded as 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0 instead of 0.1, _, 0.9, 0.5. A silently displaced stroke tail that still parsed as a real stroke.

nonFiniteVectors.name: nanEveryChannel
nonFiniteVectors.why: All six channels non-finite on a single point. Encoding must complete and the result must decode; Swift used to trap here rather than return.

nonFiniteVectors.name: nanPressureKeepsPosition
nonFiniteVectors.why: A NaN in one channel must not disturb the others on the same point. Pressure goes to zero; x and y are untouched. This is what makes coercion per-channel rather than a dropped point.

nonFiniteVectors.name: nanTimeMidStroke
nonFiniteVectors.why: The time channel is the one that already shipped a crash, and it is monotonic, so a poisoned `previous` there shifts every later timestamp by a constant and then the decoder's max(0, t) floor flattens the ones it drives negative — a stroke that replays as if part of it were drawn instantaneously.

nonFiniteVectors.name: infinitiesClamp
nonFiniteVectors.why: Infinity is a different path from NaN: comparisons against it are ordered, so the range clamp catches it and it never reaches the non-finite guard. Positions land on the range ends, t on the Int32 ceiling. Pinned so a future 'simplification' that replaces the clamp with the guard is caught.

nonFiniteVectors.name: nanTiltReadsAsChannelFloor
nonFiniteVectors.why: The one place the rule is not also the channel's own zero. Tilt's range is offset so 0 degrees sits mid-scale, so a non-finite tilt writes wire zero and decodes as -90 degrees, not 0. Deliberate: one uniform rule three implementations cannot drift on, rather than a per-channel table of sane defaults. Pinned so nobody 'fixes' it in one language.
